##### INVITED REVIEW

##### Cognition & Emotion Lecture at the 2009 ISRE Meeting

##### Emotion regulation in depression: Examining the role of cognitive processes

Jutta Joormann and Catherine D’Avanzato University of Miami, Miami, FL, USA
Sustained negative affect is a hallmark feature of depressive episodes. The ability to regulate emotional responses to negative events may therefore play a critical role in our understanding of this debilitating disorder. Individual differences in cognitive processes such as attention, memory, and interpretation may underlie difficulties in emotion regulation and numerous studies have identified cognitive biases and deficits that characterise depressed people. Few studies, however, have explicitly linked these biases to the difficulties in emotion regulation that are associated with depression. In this paper we discuss relations among cognitive processes and emotion regulation and review the depression literature to identify cognitive biases and deficits that may underlie maladaptive responses to negative events and mood states. Our review suggests that difficulties in the disengagement from negative material, memory biases, and deficits in cognitive control are frequently observed in depressive disorders and may be associated with the use of maladaptive emotion regulation strategies, such as rumination. These biases may also be related to difficulties implementing strategies that are effective for non-depressed people, such as recall of mood-incongruent material and reappraisal. Our review also suggests, however, that empirical studies linking cognitive biases and emotion regulation in depression are still largely missing and would present an important goal for future research in this area.
Keywords: Emotion regulation; Depression; Cognition; Emotion; Cognitive bias.

regulation, often defined as the ‘‘processes by which individuals influence which emotions they have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions’’ (Gross, 1998, p. 275) may inform our models of depression. Cognitive the-ories of depression, however, have not focused much on these aspects of the disorder. In trying to understand underlying mechanisms of risk for depression and maintenance of depressive episodes, these theories have focused primarily on the role of cognition and have identified mood-congruent processing biases1 that characterise currently de-pressed people and people at risk. This focus has led to improved theories of the onset and maintenance of depression and most importantly has provided critical guidelines for prevention and intervention efforts (Beck, 1976; Hollon, Stewart, & Strunk, 2006). Our most successful current depression treatment, cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), proposes that changes in cognition will lead to improvement of other symptoms of the disorder including sustained negative affect and anhedonia. Numerous studies have investigated how cognitive processes differ in depressed and non-depressed people, and whether people at risk for depression and people who have recovered from a depressive episode resemble currently depressed people in their perception of the world, their attention towards emotional aspects of their environment, and their memory for and interpretation of emo-tional material and autobiographical events (see Mathews & MacLeod, 2005; Joormann, 2008, for recent reviews). Still, an important assumption of cognitive theories of depression remains largely untested; that is the idea that these biases are, indeed, causally linked to sustained negative affect and that therefore modifying biased processing of emotional material will lead to long-lasting im-provement in depressive affect. Investigating emotion regulation in depression may help address this important question. Specifically, depression-associated differences in basic cognitive processes such as attention, memory, and interpretation may
result in the use of maladaptive emotion regulation strategies, such as rumination, and may interfere with the use of more adaptive strategies, such as reappraisal, thereby resulting in the sustained negative affect that characterises the disorder.
It is likely that there are a number of factors that affect emotion regulation in depression including knowledge about effective strategies as well as motivation to implement these strategies (Campbell-Sills & Barlow, 2007; Kring & Werner, 2004). In this paper, however, we want to focus on one specific factor that may help or hinder adaptive responding to negative affect: individual differ-ences in cognitive processes. Cognition plays a critical role in human emotion (Lazarus, 1999). According to cognitive theories of emotion, cog-nitive appraisals determine if an emotion is experi-enced and which emotion is experienced (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). Cognition, therefore, is a primary route through which emotions are regu-lated. Consequently, individual differences in attention, memory and interpretation may affect people’s ability to regulate emotion and mood states, thereby setting the stage for an increased vulnerability to emotional disorders (Joormann, Yoon, & Siemer, 2010). In the following sections, we will outline how cognitive processes may affect emotion regulation and how this may apply to depressive disorders. We believe that these con-siderations help close important gaps in current cognitive theories of depression and have important clinical implications.
COGNITIVE PROCESSES, EMOTION, AND EMOTION REGULATION
The idea that people do not just passively experi-ence their emotions but rather actively respond to them and have the ability to modify them has become widely accepted. Ranging from research on emotion-focused coping by Lazarus to Gross’s

JOORMANN AND D’AVANZATO
914 COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6)
process model of emotion regulation, publications discussing definitions of this important ability and mechanisms underlying emotion regulation have increased exponentially over the past years (see Koole, 2009, for a recent review). Still, defining and differentiating emotion and emotion regulation is difficult even though some authors have recently begun to formulate core features of these concepts (Gross, 2002; Gross & Thompson, 2007; see Bloch, Moran, & Kring, 2009, for a discussion of different definitions of emotion regulation). Emo-tions are seen as a response to a specific situation (internal or external) or as a person situation transaction (Lazarus, 1991; Scherer, 1984). Emo-tions change over time in response to changing demands of the situation and the coping attempts of the person. Situational demands or changes in the situation compel the person to attend to an event, and this attention results in specific apprai-sals, which in turn lead to emotional responses to the situation that are caused by and correspond to the appraisal pattern (see Lazarus, 1999; Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). Appraisal theories of emotion state that the cognitive appraisal of a situation, not the situation itself, determines the quality and intensity of the emotional response (Ellsworth & Scherer, 2003; Scherer, 2001; Siemer, Mauss, & Gross, 2007). These theories propose that emotional events are interpreted along a number of appraisal dimensions including importance, expectedness, responsibility, and the degree of controllability, which determine whether an emo-
tion is experienced and which emotion is experi-enced (Lazarus, 1991; Ortony, Clore, & Collins, 1988). In support of these theories, research has found that people exposed to the same event display a wide variety of emotional responses depending on their appraisals of the event (e.g., Siemer et al., 2007). This sequence of attention and appraisal is seen as a recursive loop that can be entered at any point. It is possible, for example, that the situation did not change, but that the person suddenly pays attention to certain aspects of it that are likely to elicit certain appraisals, or that the appraisal of the situation is otherwise modified, which will result in an emotional response. It is also possible that an emotional response itself changes the appraisal of the situation, for example by changing attentional deployment to certain aspects of the event. Emo-tional responses may also change the situation, which then changes appraisals of the situation, and so forth. It is furthermore possible that a situation is already entered with a pre-existing emotional state, which affects the appraisal of the situation (Lerner & Keltner, 2000; Siemer, 2001, 2005a).
It is critical to keep the recursive nature of emotion generation and regulation processes in mind because this implies that there are numerous entry points at which people can intervene to modify their emotional responses. Accordingly, Gross (2002) has presented a model in which emotion regulation can take place at any point in the emotion generation sequence (see Figure 1).
