COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6) 915
for example, are emotion regulation strategies that affect the emotion-eliciting situation directly. Use of these strategies can be very effective because the emotion-eliciting aspects of the situation are avoided or modified early on in the emotion-generation sequence, possibly prior to the generation of an emotional response. Similarly, attentional deployment, involving directing attention towards or away from the emotion-eliciting aspects of the situation, is a regulation strategy that influences the appraisal of a situation and determines whether the situation will be appraised in an emotion-generating fashion. Cognitive change or reappraisal modifies appraisals directly, whereas response mod-ulation, such as expression suppression, changes the response to the emotion elicited by the appraisal. Whereas cognitive reappraisal involves the reinter-pretation of the emotion-eliciting situation in a way that changes the potential emotional response, expressive suppression involves inhibiting the beha-vioural expression of the emotion experience. This brief discussion of the emotion generation sequence and the steps at which emotion regulation takes place clearly reveals the central importance of cognition. At least two steps in the sequence, attentional deployment and reappraisal, make it necessary to pay close attention to processes such as attention, interpretation, and memory. Indeed, recent studies*building upon early work by Lazarus (1964)*demonstrate that voluntary changes of the appraisals of a situation can change the intensity of an emotional reaction (Gross, 1998; Ochsner, Bunge, Gross, & Gabrieli, 2002). Moreover, it is noteworthy that non-cognitive emotion regulation strategies, such as inhibition of emotion expressions, have been consistently found to be less effective than strategies that affect cognition (Gross, 1998; Gross & Levenson, 1997).
Before discussing this in more detail we should point out, however, that most of the processes we have talked about so far can be initiated strategi-cally or can occur automatically. Given the crucial role of automatic processes in cognition and emotion, emotion generation and regulation can take place at a much faster pace and be less accessible to conscious thought than the above discussion of the emotion generation sequence
suggests. Automaticity of the involved (cognitive) processes can make it difficult to separate the components of the described sequence, and also complicates the separation of emotion generation from emotion regulation. Indeed, emotion reg-ulation may often require that an automatic, that is, fast and unconscious appraisal of a situation be replaced with a more controlled evaluation of the circumstance, meaning, and consequences of the event (Siemer & Reisenzein, 2007). Whereas emotion regulation is often strategically initiated, it can also take place without the person’s knowl-edge or intention, which further adds to the difficulties in differentiating emotion generation and emotion regulation (Mauss, Cook, & Gross, 2007). The role of automatic regulation processes in emotional disorders is an important area for future research in psychopathology.
Empirical research addressing these concepts needs to separate individual differences in basic cognitive processes from emotional response and emotion regulation. To separate emotion regula-tion from emotion generation researchers need to demonstrate that an emotional response was pre-sent in the first place that was somehow changed, truncated or terminated as a result of emotion regulation. According to Gross (1998): ‘‘Emotion regulation must be inferred when an emotional response would have proceeded in one fashion but instead is observed to proceed in another’’ (p. 286). Emotion regulation, however, can sometimes be employed so early in the emotion generation sequence that the emotional response is prevented from occurring (anticipatory emotion regulation). In this case, researchers have to demonstrate that if the person had behaved differently (i.e., not used the emotion regulation strategy or had employed a different strategy), an emotional response would have occurred. Clearly, researchers cannot attribute the absence of (or differences in) emo-tional reactions to emotion regulation without this additional evidence. Even though the occurrence of anticipatory or automatic emotion regulation may be difficult to prove in individual cases, differen-tiating emotion generation and regulation clearly is critical if we want to investigate these processes in an empirically meaningful way. If simply having an
JOORMANN AND D’AVANZATO
916 COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6)
emotional response is taken as an indicator of (the lack of) emotion regulation, but not having an emotional response is also taken as an indicator of emotion regulation, this concept becomes mean-ingless and research becomes tautological.
Likewise, it is important to separate individual differences in basic cognitive processes from emotion generation and emotion regulation in response to an emotion-eliciting event. We pro-pose in this paper that biases in the processing of emotional material that can be observed in cogni-tive tasks administered outside of specific mood states or stress challenges predict the use and effectiveness of regulation strategies people em-ploy when experiencing emotional responses to a stressful situation. Examining this relation re-quires that studies combine cognitive tasks that assess individual differences in cognitive proces-sing with assessments of affective states in response to mood challenges and with the assess-ment of the use of emotion regulation strategies. The use and effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies such as reappraisal and attentional deployment may depend heavily on individual differences in basic cognitive processes such as cognitive control and the ability to disengage attention from emotional material. Cognitive biases in perception and attention may lead to inflexible, automatic, and unconscious apprai-sals that make it difficult to regulate emotions by using deliberate reappraisal of the situation (Siemer & Reisenzein, 2007). Individual differ-ences in these processes may also be associated with the use of strategies that do not fit the situation. Implicit memory for traumatic events, for example, may alert the individual and lead to situation selection or situation modification even though the situation is not dangerous and may not elicit the degree of negative affect that is expected. Thus, it is important to investigate the role of individual differences in attention, memory and interpretation in emotion regulation because they can affect the selection of strategies and the effectiveness of regulation.
Given that cognition is such an intricate part of the emotion experience, it is interesting to note the relative scarcity of research that investigates
the relation of individual differences in cognitive processes, emotion generation, and emotion reg-ulation in emotional disorders. Even though research on cognitive aspects of disorders has increased dramatically over the past decades, rarely do studies investigate whether cognitive processes are causal in generating difficulties in emotion regulation. We know, for example, that depression is associated with biased processing of negative information, but very few studies have tried to link research on cognitive biases in this disorder to the hallmark feature of depression, which is sustained negative affect. Even fewer studies have investi-gated whether these biases are related to the use and effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies. Simply demonstrating that people who are diag-nosed with emotional disorders differ from control samples in their cognitive processes is not sufficient evidence that these processes are causing specific emotions or emotion dysregulation. Making ex-plicit the link among individual differences in basic cognitive processes, emotional experience and regulation in depression will therefore be a main aim of this article but will often remain speculative given overlap in the definitions of these constructs and the lack of empirical studies that target both cognition and emotion at the same time. Before taking a closer look at cognitive processes that help or hinder emotion regulation, we want to briefly review research on emotion regulation in depression.
EMOTION REGULATION IN DEPRESSION
Surprisingly few studies have investigated the use and effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies in clinical depression. Moreover, most of these studies have relied on self-report data and have examined people who score high on depression inventories instead of diagnosed samples. Still, the findings of these studies support the claim that a more frequent use of certain strategies (e.g., emotion suppression, rumination) and a less frequent use of other strategies (e.g., re-appraisal) are related to depression symptoms (Campbell-Sills, Barlow, Brown & Hofman,
EMOTION REGULATION IN DEPRESSION
COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6) 917
2006; Garnefski & Kraaij, 2006, 2007; Gross & John, 2003).
In addition, recent studies suggest that impaired emotion regulation does not only characterise currently depressed people but can be obse-rved after recovery. Ehring, Fischer, Schnülle, Bösterling, and Tuschen-Caffier (2008), for ex-ample, found that recovered depressed participants compared to control participants reported greater difficulties regulating their negative emotions and more frequent use of rumination (Ehring et al., 2008). The groups, however, did not differ on positive reappraisal or positive refocusing, which led the authors to propose that difficulties with reapprai-sal are only observed in currently depressed people.
Although it is difficult to categorise a specific regulation strategy as maladaptive without taking into account the context in which the strategy is used, numerous studies have demonstrated that the habitual use of particular strategies, primarily reappraisal and expressive suppression, is associated with positive and negative outcomes, respectively. Indeed, habitual use of reappraisal versus expressive suppression has been shown to be associated with the experience and expression of greater positive affect and lesser negative affect, better interpersonal functioning, and increased well-being (Gross & John, 2003). In a recent study, participants diag-nosed with depression were less likely to endorse the use of reappraisal but did not differ from the control group in their self-reported use of expres-sive suppression (Joormann & Gotlib, 2010). No study so far has investigated the effectiveness of reappraisal in a clinically depressed sample. A particularly noteworthy study, however, has examined neural correlates of reappraisal in this disorder. Johnstone, van Reekum, Urry, Kalin, and Davidson (2007) reported that during reappraisal of emotional pictures, non-depressed individuals showed a correlation between increased dorso-lateral prefontral cortex (DLPFC) activation and decreased amygdala response mediated by the ventro-medial prefontral cortex (VMPFC), whereas depressed individuals did not show this pattern, suggesting difficulties in recruiting brain regions involved in cognitive control to regulate emotions.
An emotion regulation strategy that may alleviate negative mood in the short term but may have long-term detrimental effects is thought suppression. Several studies suggest that depressed and previously depressed people are more likely to use thought suppression and that the use of this strategy may play an important role in the onset and maintenance of depression (Wenzlaff, Rude, Taylor, Stoltz, & Sweatt, 2001; Wenzlaff, Rude, & West, 2002). Kircanski, Craske, and Bjork (2008), for example, found that individuals with high levels of trait anxiety who were assigned to a thought-suppression condition exhibited in-creased memory for threat words compared to thought-concentration and thought-wandering conditions. If persistent attempts to suppress unwanted thoughts lead to a subsequent increase in such thoughts or an enhanced recall of negative events, this may serve to increase rumination, thereby maintaining negative mood. Indeed, Beevers and Meyer (2008) found that suppression after a negative mood induction increased the accessibility of negative thoughts, even after the dysphoric mood had subsided. In contrast, a recent study reported that depressed participants were able to reduce their negative affect with the use of emotion suppression, supporting the proposition that suppression may at least bring short-term relief for depressed people (Liverant, Brown, Barlow, & Roemer, 2008).
When experiencing an unpleasant mood state, people may attempt to regulate their mood by retrieving pleasant thoughts and memories, thereby reducing or even reversing a negative mood-congruency effect (Erber & Erber, 1994; Josephson, Singer, & Salovey, 1996; Parrott & Sabini, 1990). Interestingly, researchers have iden-tified individual differences that seem to moderate the use of this strategy. Smith and Petty (1995), for example, showed that in response to a negative mood induction, participants low in self-esteem exhibited mood-congruent recall, but subjects high in self-esteem did not. Moreover, the more negative high self-esteem subjects felt, the more positive were their cognitions (mood-incongruent recall). Likewise, Joormann and Siemer (2004) showed that dysphoric participants had reduced
JOORMANN AND D’AVANZATO
918 COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6)
accessibility to mood-incongruent material after a negative mood induction. In a related study, Joormann, Siemer, and Gotlib (2007a) demon-strated that depressed participants could not use positive autobiographical memories to repair ne-gative affect. Thus, the results of these studies imply that depression may affect the use of mood-incongruent material to repair negative affect.
The majority of studies investigating emotion regulation in depression, however, have focused on rumination. According to Nolen-Hoeksema and her collaborators, rumination is a particularly detrimental response to negative affect that hinders recovery from negative mood and prolongs depres-sive episodes (Nolen-Hoeksema, Wisco, & Lyubomirsky, 2008). What characterises rumina-tion and differentiates it from negative automatic thoughts is that it is a style of thought rather than just negative content (Nolen-Hoeksema, 1991; Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008). Thus, rumination is defined by the process of recurring thoughts and ideas, often described as a ‘‘recycling’’ of thoughts, and not necessarily by the content of these recurring thoughts. In an extensive programme of experi-mental and correlational studies, Nolen-Hoeksema and colleagues investigated rumination in depres-sion and dysphoria and analysed how this response style exacerbates sad moods and predicts future depressive episodes (e.g., Morrow & Nolen-Hoeksema, 1990). Self-reported levels of rumina-tion have been found to predict higher levels of dysphoria over time in prospective studies with non-clinical samples, even after controlling for initial differential depression levels (e.g., Nolen-Hoeksema & Morrow, 1991). Moreover, studies have shown that rumination predicts higher levels of depressive symptoms and onset of major depressive episodes, and mediates the gender difference in depressive symptoms (Nolen-Hoeksema, 2000; Nolen-Hoeksema, Stice, Wade, & Bohon, 2007). Research also indicates that rumination enhances cognitive biases (e.g., Lyubomirksy & Nolen-Hoeksema, 1995). Thus, dysphoric participants who were induced to ruminate endorsed more negative interpretations of hypothetical situations, generated less effective problem-solving strategies (Lyubomirksy &
Nolen-Hoeksema, 1995), and showed increased recall of negative autobiographical memories (Lyubomirsky, Caldwell, & Nolen-Hoeksema, 1998). Similarly, Singer and Dobson (2007) found that remitted depressed patients who were in-structed to ruminate during a negative mood induction had higher levels of depressed mood as compared to participants who were instructed to use distraction. It is important to keep in mind, however, that there is discussion about the nature of rumination that suggests that rumination can be adaptive depending on the thought content, the context in which it occurs, and the use of abstract versus concrete processing while ruminat-ing (see Watkins, 2008, for a recent review).
In contrast to rumination, distraction is often thought of as an adaptive regulation strategy. Studies have reported that depressed participants are less likely to use distraction even though they state that it could help them alleviate their negative affect (Lyubomirsky & Nolen-Hoeksema, 1993). Indeed, in studies with both depressed patients and non-depressed samples, participants who dis-tracted themselves from their sad mood by com-pleting an emotionally neutral task were able to attenuate their negative affect (Erber & Tesser, 1992; Nolen-Hoeksema & Morrow, 1991). Simi-larly, in a group of depressed adolescents, Park and colleagues found that participants induced to use distraction by reading about 45 externally focused neutral items decreased their depressed mood as compared to participants who focused on more emotional, self-focused items (Park, Goodyer, & Teasdale, 2004). Other studies have reported that dysphoric, clinically depressed, and recovered depressed people are able to use distraction to repair an induced negative mood state (Joormann & Siemer, 2004; Joormann et al., 2007a). In addition, Lavender and Watkins (2004) reported that distraction compared to rumination was associated with less negative future oriented thinking in a depressed sample. Whereas these laboratory studies suggest that distraction reduces negative affect, the positive effects associated with distraction may not be long lasting. Kross and Ayduk (2008), for example, found that distraction decreased de-pressed mood immediately after a mood induction.
EMOTION REGULATION IN DEPRESSION
COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6) 919
In follow-up sessions one day and seven days later, the positive effects of distraction had disappeared and levels of self-reported depressed mood had significantly increased relative to a control group. The authors explained these results by pointing out that distraction does nothing to change how emotional experiences are dealt with in future situations; thus the utility of distraction appears to be limited to the short term (Kross & Ayduk, 2008). This explanation is similar to Campbell-Sills’ proposition that distraction is simply a ‘‘band-aid’’ approach rather than a long-term solution to excessive anxiety and/or depression (Campbell-Sills’ & Barlow, 2007). Indeed, other research suggests that distraction may not just be ineffective, but that it may even be detrimental in the long term. For instance, individuals who use avoidance coping strategies such as distraction when they are stressed are more likely to develop depression (Felsten, 2002; Holahan, Moos, Holahan, Brennan, & Schutte, 2005; Powers, Gallagher-Thompson, & Kraemer, 2002). It may be important to distinguish between different ways of distraction to address the question of whether it is an adaptive or maladaptive strategy. Thus, the active avoidance to think ‘‘realistically’’ about a problem combined with behavioural avoidance of addressing the problem assessed by Holahan et al. (2005) may differ from the use of more benign distraction strategies that may help people cope with the immediate impact of the situation, thus allowing them to more effec-tively use other strategies, such as reappraisal, at a later point in time (Yoon & Joormann, 2009).
Taken together, the reviewed studies clearly suggest that depressed and non-depressed people differ in the use and maybe also in the effectiveness of certain emotion regulation strategies. There is still debate, however, about whether many of these strategies can be can easily characterised as adaptive or maladaptive (see Watkins, 2008, for a recent discussion of this issue with regard to rumination). Mechanisms underlying these differences in emo-tion regulation remain to be explored. In the next sections we examine individual differences in basic cognitive processes that may hinder or help emo-tion regulation as well as their relation to depres-sion. We should also keep in mind, however, that
depression and other forms of psychopathology may not so much be associated with the use of emotion regulation strategies that differ dramati-cally from strategies employed by other people but rather that it is the inflexible use of certain strategies, the poor fit of the regulation strategy with the situation, and differences in the ability to implement effective strategies that are important. Empirical studies are needed to investigate this proposition. Exploring individual differences in cognitive processes may help us understand how these difficulties are associated with depression. Taking Gross’s process model of emotion regula-tion as the starting point, the following sections review cognitive biases and deficits that have been observed in depression and link them to difficulties in emotion regulation at the various stages of the emotion generation sequence (see Figure 1).
PERCEPTION AND ATTENTION
The easiest and probably most effective way to regulate emotions is to avoid the emotion-eliciting situation, to ignore the cues that elicit the emotion, or to attend to the situation initially but to quickly disengage from it and redirect attention. It is important to note that the emotion-eliciting cues can be present in the person such as bodily sensations and thoughts (internal) or in the outside world such as pictures of an ex-girlfriend (ex-ternal). These strategies are so effective that it may be difficult to evaluate whether emotion regulation did indeed occur. Individual differences in the ability to disengage attention from emotional material, however, may make it difficult to use attentional deployment when confronted with a potentially emotion-eliciting situation. Individual differences in perception and attention can also influence the selection and effectiveness of other emotion regulation strategies such as situation selection and modification. A person who is likely to spot the one frowning face in the crowd may leave the party early or refrain from engaging in conversation, anticipating the negative emotional response at being criticised when stating an opinion. Further complicating things, attention
JOORMANN AND D’AVANZATO
920 COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6)
and perception biases in these cases may operate at an automatic level, leading people to avoid or modify situations unintentionally and without proper evaluation of the situation and of the probability that it will indeed elicit the emotion one strives to avoid.
Individual differences in early perception of emotional material and in the tendency to orient towards these stimuli, as well as a person’s ability to disengage from emotional stimuli, are impor-tant factors that may influence emotion regulation when confronted with an emotion-eliciting situa-tion. Not surprisingly, there is ample evidence that individual differences in these cognitive processes are associated with different forms of psychopathology. Disorders differ in whether automatic processing biases and early perception of emotional cues are an issue, whether people demonstrate attentional biases towards emotional material, or whether they have difficulties disen-gaging from this material. Enhanced perception of emotional stimuli may frequently elicit the use of anticipatory emotion regulation strategies such as situation selection and modification. Automatic processing biases that lead to the early detection of emotional stimuli and guide attention towards the processing of these stimuli may make it difficult to strategically disengage attention. These processes in turn increase the probability that certain appraisals will follow.
The question of whether depression is asso-ciated with enhanced and maybe even automatic perception of emotional stimuli has been investi-gated in studies using either subliminal material, material with low degrees of emotional intensity or very fast presentation times. Studies have employed disorder-specific material or material that is relevant to emotion across disorders, such as facial expressions of emotion. Numerous stu-dies have provided evidence for the processing of subliminally presented anxiety-provoking stimuli in anxiety disorders using a number of tasks (e.g., Bradley, Mogg, Millar, & White, 1995; Mogg, Millar & Bradley 2000). Strikingly, few studies to date have found similar biases in clinically de-pressed participants when depression-relevant (or other) stimuli have been masked in order to
investigate unconscious processing (see Mathews & MacLeod, 2005, for a recent review).
Mogg, Bradley, Williams, and Mathews (1993), for example, used a modified Stroop task and presented anxiety-related, depression-related, positive, and neutral words either subliminally (followed by a mask) or supraliminally. In the emotional Stroop task, individuals with depres-sion should take longer to respond to the colour of the negative words compared to neutral words suggesting that their attention was ‘‘grabbed’’ by the content of the words. Whereas anxious participants exhibited slower colour naming of all negative words at both subliminal and supra-liminal exposure durations, depressed participants did not differ from control participants in the subliminal condition (see also Lim & Kim, 2005). Similarly, Yovel and Mineka (2005) failed to find a relation between Stroop biases for subliminally presented depression-related words and self-reported depressive symptoms in a sample of undergraduate students.
Several investigators have used the dot-probe task with briefly presented and masked emotional words to investigate automatic processing biases in depression. In the dot-probe task, a pair of stimuli (words or faces) is presented simultaneously: one stimulus is neutral and the other is emotional. Participants are asked to respond to a probe that replaces the neutral or the emotional stimulus. Allocation of attention to the spatial position of the stimuli is determined from response latencies to the probes. Here, too, the results have not been encouraging (e.g., Mogg, Bradley, & Williams, 1995). Bradley, Mogg, and Lee (1997) reported that, whereas induced or naturally occurring sad mood was associated with increased attention to negative words at long exposure durations, there was no effect when the words were presented briefly and masked (Bradley et al., 1997; see also Donaldson, Lam, & Mathews, 2007).
A number of studies have used facial expressions of emotion to investigate whether depressed participants are particularly prone to perceive sadness or anger in other people. Facial expressions of emotion are powerful stimuli that represent salient features of the social environment (e.g.,
EMOTION REGULATION IN DEPRESSION
COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6) 921
Ekman & Friesen, 1976; Hansen & Hansen, 1994). Misreading facial expressions particularly when they are subtle can have profound conse-quences for the interpretation of a situation and may thereby affect emotional responding and the selection of regulation strategies. Whereas some investigators have found that depressed individuals are characterised by deficits in the processing of all emotional (and neutral) facial expressions (e.g., Carton, Kessler, & Pape, 1999), other researchers have failed to corroborate this finding (e.g., Ridout, Astell, Reid, Glen, & O’Carroll, 2003). Numerous investigators have found depression to be associated with negative biases in the processing of specific types of emotional faces (e.g., Hale, 1998). The question of whether depression is characterised by early perception of emotional expressions has been examined in studies using subtle expressions of emotion. These studies suggest that depression is associated primarily with difficul-ties identifying subtle positive emotional expres-sions, but depressed individuals do not more easily identify low intensity sadness (Joormann & Gotlib, 2006; Surguladze et al., 2004).
Taken together, empirical findings that de-pression is associated with the easy identification of mood-congruent material or a fast orienting towards negative stimuli are rather mixed. Based on such findings, Williams, Watts, MacLeod, and Mathews (1997) proposed that depressed persons are not characterised by early processing biases. These authors suggested that depressive biases are observed in strategic elaboration and make it difficult for depressed people to disengage from negative material. If attention at later stages of processing is biased towards emotional material, the use of attention redirection as an emotion regulation strategy may be difficult.
Indeed, there is increasing evidence that de-pressed persons are characterised by attentional biases in later stages of processing. Recent studies using the dot-probe task, for example, have reported selective attention in depression but only under conditions of long stimuli exposures (e.g., Bradley et al., 1997; Donaldson et al., 2007; Joormann & Gotlib, 2007). In two studies, Joormann, Talbot, and Gotlib (2007b) replicated
these findings in samples of remitted depressed adults and non-disordered girls at high risk for depression due to their mothers’ psychopathology (see also Joormann & Gotlib, 2007). These findings suggest that attentional biases are not simply a symptom of depression or a scar of a previous depressive episode but may play an important role in the vulnerability to depression.
Overall, these results suggest that depressed individuals do not direct their attention to negative information more frequently than do control participants, but once it captures their attention they exhibit difficulties in disengaging from it. Whereas the dot-probe task has been criticised as a measure of disengagement, similar difficulties in disengaging attention from negative material have now been demonstrated in various attention tasks (Koster, DeRaedt, Goelven, Franck, & Crombez, 2005). Rinck and Becker (2005) reported that depressed participants did not show enhanced detection of depression-related words in a visual search task, but were more easily distracted by negative words. Eizenman et al. (2003) used eye-tracking tech-nology to continuously monitor point of gaze. Depressed individuals spent significantly more time looking at pictures featuring sadness and loss and had significantly longer average glance durations for these pictures than did non-depressed controls. Similarly, Caseras, Garner, Bradley, and Mogg (2007) found in an eye-tracking study that depressed individuals were no more likely than controls to shift their attention toward negative stimuli, but once their attention was focused on negative stimuli they spent significantly more time looking at these stimuli than non-depressed controls.
We discussed previously that simply showing that emotional disorders are associated with cognitive biases provides little support for the proposition that these processes play a role in emotion regulation. A link among cognitive biases and emotional responding has been reported in studies that have examined whether individual differences in attention biases are associated with mood changes in response to exposure to a stressor. Compton, Heller, Banich, Palmieri, and
JOORMANN AND D’AVANZATO
922 COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6)
Miller (2000), for example, demonstrated that a reduced ability to disengage attention was asso-ciated with increased reactivity to a distressing film clip. Individual differences in orienting, however, were not related to the mood response. Beevers and Carver (2003) demonstrated that changes in attentional bias for negative but not positive words following a negative mood induc-tion interacted with life stress to predict onset of depressive symptoms in college students. Like-wise, MacLeod and Hagan (1992) found that women who displayed the most pronounced bias towards negative information later reported the greatest amount of distress upon learning that they had been diagnosed with cervical cancer.
Whereas the previous studies report associa-tions between individual differences in cognitive biases and emotional responses to stressors, Ellenbogen, Schwartzman, Stewart, and Walker (2002) examined more directly whether atten-tional deployment while exposed to a stressor predicted emotional responding. These authors found that people under a negative stress induction were faster to shift attention away from negative words compared to positive and neutral words and that these attentional shifts were associated with mood changes in response to the stressor. The Ellenbogen et al. study supports the proposition that attentional deployment is an effective emo-tion regulation strategy. These authors reported further that people with elevated depression scores had difficulties shifting attention away from emotional stimuli. In a related study, these authors showed that the ability to disengage from supra-liminally presented dysphoric pictures was asso-ciated with changes in negative mood ratings in response to a subsequent stress task but did not affect neuroendocrine responding. In contrast, rapid disengagement from masked threat pictures affected neuroendocrine responding to the stres-sor but not mood (Ellenbogen, Schwartzman, Stewart, & Walker, 2006). Likewise, Johnson (2009a) demonstrated that participants who took longer to switch their attention from neutral to emotional material exhibited higher trait anxiety and more worrying. In addition, participants who switched faster to the emotional material were
more frustrated by a stressful task. Johnson (2009b) also found that participants who were better able to focus on happy and avoid angry faces in a dot-probe task were less frustrated and worked harder in a stressful anagram task.
Whereas these studies suggest that individual differences in cognitive biases and individual differences in the employment of an emotion regulation strategy (i.e., attentional deployment) are associated with emotional responding, a more direct proof for the causal role of cognitive biases in emotion generation and regulation would require evidence that changes in cognitive pro-cesses are related to changes in emotional states. The only set of studies that provides this more direct test comes from recent work on cognitive bias modification. These studies aimed to train people to overcome biased cognitive processes, which should enable them to use emotion regula-tion strategies more effectively thereby changing emotional responding. Importantly, these studies employed control groups that did not undergo the training, which allowed the authors to conclude that the training led to changes in emotional responding in the experimental compared to the control group. These studies demonstrated, for example, that training highly anxious people to disengage their attention from threat material leads to changes in mood and reduced reactivity to stressful events. In a typical training paradigm, the dot probe is presented more consistently after the non-threat-relevant stimuli (rather than equally following threat and non-threat stimuli), so that participants learn to attend to neutral stimuli and away from threat stimuli. Using this approach, MacLeod, Rutherford, Campbell, Ebsworthy, and Holker (2002) first established that atten-tional biases could be modified by working with participants who scored in the middle third of the distribution on the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI; Spielberger, Gorusch, & Lushene, 1971). They found that, following attentional training away from threat, participants reported reduced negative affect to a standardised stress manipula-tion. Unfortunately, this study did not test whether the training group did, indeed, show changes in attentional deployment when
EMOTION REGULATION IN DEPRESSION
COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6) 923
confronted with the stressor. They did demon-strate, however, that the changes in emotional responding were mediated by the training-in-duced changes in biases. Thus, these results provide support for the proposition that changes in biases lead to changes in emotional responding, but it remains unclear whether an improved ability to use a specific emotion regulation strategy when under stress is the underlying mechanism of change. A more recent study of attentional bias training extended MacLeod’s findings by showing that positive attentional biases can also be trained (Wadlinger & Isaacowitz, 2008). Importantly, in this study, the authors did, indeed, test whether changes in bias led to changes in the use of emotion regulation strate-gies when exposed to a stressor. Specifically, participants who had been trained to attend to positive stimuli subsequently looked less at nega-tive images during a stress induction (Wadlinger & Isaacowitz, 2008). This study to date provides the most direct test of the idea that individual differences in attention biases lead to changes in the use of emotion regulation strategies, which in turn modifies emotional responding. Based on these findings, researchers have begun to examine attentional training with clinical samples, but no studies thus far have examined whether modifying cognitive biases in depressed participants leads to changes in the use or effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies and thus to changes in emotional responding.
What are the implications of these depression-related biases in perception and attention for emotion regulation? Depression does not seem to be characterised by high sensitivity towards the detection of emotion-eliciting stimuli, which could result in anticipatory emotion regulation charac-terised by avoidance behaviour (situation selection) and the use of safety strategies (situation modifica-tion). Instead, depression is mostly associated with difficulties in using attentional disengagement. Difficulties disengaging from negative stimuli may preclude depressed people from using effective emotion regulation strategies such as distraction and attentional avoidance when confronted with stressful events and may result in the sustained
processing of emotion eliciting stimuli, leading to prolonged negative affect. In addition, attentional biases towards negative material may interfere with a person’s ability to successfully reframe emotion-eliciting events. Being ‘‘stuck’’ in attending to negative aspects of the situation may make it more difficult to shift attention to more positive aspects, thus hindering a more balanced appraisal of the emotion-eliciting event.
INTERPRETATION AND APPRAISAL
Most situations that evoke emotions are ambig-uous. How cues in these situations are initially interpreted and appraised determines the emo-tional response and determines whether this response is appropriate in this situation or not. Does the frowning face in the audience mean that the presentation was a failure? Does the fact that I am not invited to the party mean that my friend does not like me? Did the person in front of me intentionally step on my foot? Reinterpretation or reappraisal is a potent emotion regulation strategy because it allows flexible emotional responding without changing the situation and without ignoring the emotion-eliciting cues. Biases in interpretation, especially when they are automatic, can make it difficult to use reappraisal (Siemer & Reisenzein, 2007) and can lead to inflexible and inappropriate responding. Interpretation biases and automatic appraisal processes associated with depressive disorders, for example, could result in rigid, automatic mood-congruent inter-pretations of potentially emotion-eliciting events and may make it difficult to see the situation from a different perspective or to entertain alternative interpretations. Results, however, are mixed with regard to whether depression is characterised by automatic interpretation biases (Lawson, MacLeod, & Hammond, 2002). Butler and Mathews (1983), for example, presented clinically depressed participants with ambiguous scenarios and found that, compared to non-depressed participants, depressed individuals ranked nega-tive interpretations higher than they did other possible interpretations. In a study assessing biases
JOORMANN AND D’AVANZATO
924 COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6)
using response latencies to target words that were presented after ambiguous sentences, no inter-pretation bias was found (Lawson & MacLeod, 1999). Using a similar task, Bisson and Sears (2007) failed to find evidence of an interpretive bias in depression even after a negative mood induction. Lawson et al. (2002) also examined startle magnitude during imagery elicited by emotionally ambiguous text. Using this measure, these authors reported evidence for more negative interpretations in their depressed sample and concluded that the failure to find a bias in previous studies was due to the use of response latencies. Rude, Wenzlaff, Gibbs, Vane, and Whitney (2002) demonstrated that a measure of interpretation bias, the Scrambled Sentences Test, predicted increases in depressive symptoms after 4 6 weeks in a large sample of undergra-duate students, especially when administered under cognitive load. Furthermore, a recent study reported a negative interpretation bias in never-disordered daughters of depressed mothers, pro-viding evidence for a role of these biases in increasing risk for depression onset (Dearing & Gotlib, 2009). Clearly, further studies are needed that investigate interpretive biases in depression.
Studies using self-report measures of attribu-tion have reported numerous findings that depres-sion is associated with dysfunctional attitudes and a specific attributional style that may lead to the interpretation of specific situations in depression-relevant ways and may make it difficult to re-appraise. Researchers investigating the role of dysfunctional attitudes and attributional style have relied almost exclusively on self-report mea-sures, specifically the Dysfunctional Attitude Scale (DAS) and the Cognitive Styles Questionnaire (CSQ). The DAS is a 40-item self-report measure that assesses maladaptive cognitions like perfec-tionist standards and concerns about being eval-uated by others (Weissman & Beck, 1978). The CSQ is a modified version of the Attributional Styles Questionnaire (ASQ; Peterson et al., 1982) that assesses the tendency to respond to positive and negative events with internal, stable, and global attributions (Alloy et al., 2000). Numerous studies in which these and other questionnaires
were administered to depressed and non-depressed participants have reported associations among dysfunctional attitudes, attributional styles, and other negative cognitions in currently depressed adults (Alloy, Abramson, & Francis, 1999; Fresco, Alloy, & Reilly Harrington, 2006), adolescents, and children (see Ingram, Nelson, Steidtmann, & Bistricky, 2007, for a recent review). Moreover, studies have shown that an interaction of rumina-tion with dysfunctional attitudes and attributional style predicted depressive symptoms at follow-up (Ciesla & Roberts, 2002, 2007). Watkins (2004) reported that certain types of appraisals (need to understand a situation) were associated with greater rumination. In addition, research on cog-nitive reactivity has shown that remitted depressed participants show similar styles of attribution when exposed to a negative mood induction (see Scher, Ingram, & Segal, 2005, for a recent review). Unfortunately, given that almost all of these studies have used self-report, response biases and demand characteristics need to be kept in mind as alternative explanations for differences between depressed and non-depressed participants.
As outlined previously, identifying cognitive biases in emotional disorders is not sufficient to show that these biases are, indeed, related to problems in emotion regulation, particularly if no measures of affective states are included. Recently, researchers have begun to modify interpretive biases in the hopes of modifying emotional responding. Mathews and Mackintosh (2000) used ambiguous scenarios to train individuals to make either positive (non-anxious) or negative (anxious) interpretations of ambiguous text. The authors used the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory State (STAI-S) to compare state levels of anxiety prior to and after the training and reported that participants in the negative training condition displayed elevated levels of anxiety, whereas those in the positive training condition demonstrated decreased symptoms of anxiety, supporting the hypothesis that interpretive biases play a causal role in anxiety levels. Yiend, Mackintosh, and Mathews (2005) demonstrated that the effects of interpretive training on anxiety were still present after a 24-hour delay between the training and
EMOTION REGULATION IN DEPRESSION
COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6) 925
a subsequent test. In a related study, participants
who received interpretive training using ambig-
uous homophones were subsequently presented four distressing television clips of real-life
emergency rescue situations (Wilson, MacLeod,
Mathews, & Rutherford, 2006). Participants who
were trained to interpret ambiguity in a non-
threatening manner had an attenuated anxiety
reaction to the subsequent video stressor (see also
Mackintosh, Mathews, Yiend, Ridgeway, & Cook, 2006). Recently, Beard and Amir (2008)
reported that changes in negative emotion were
mediated by training-induced changes in negative
interpretive style. These results suggest that
changes in interpretation biases can, indeed, lead
to changes in emotional responding. Unfortu-
nately, no studies so far have investigated whether changes in interpretive biases in these training
studies lead to changes in emotional responding by
affecting people’s ability to use reappraisal when
confronted with emotion-eliciting situations.
Thus, these studies show that interpretive biases
can lead to changes in emotional responding but
do not show that changes in the use or effective-ness of reappraisal is the mechanism underlying
this change. In addition, previous studies have
focused primarily on anxiety, and no studies so far
have investigated whether modifying interpretive
biases in depression affects emotional responding.
To summarise, the described studies suggest that
depression is characterised by biases in interpreta-tion and appraisals. These biases can lead to
automatic appraisals of emotion-eliciting situa-
tions and make it difficult to regulate emotions by
deliberately reappraising the situation. The evi-
dence so far provides little evidence for automatic
interpretive biases in depression but self-report
studies indicate that depression is characterised by a specific pessimistic style of attribution. These
findings also suggest that cognitive processes that
hinder emotion regulation may only become
obvious after people have been exposed to a
negative mood state. Studies that directly link
interpretive biases to difficulties in reappraisal are an important area for future research.
MEMORY
Memories affect emotion in important ways. Mood-incongruent recall is often used as a mood-repair strategy in response to a negative mood induction (e.g., Rusting & DeHart, 2000). Recent studies have demonstrated that memories of un-pleasant, compared to pleasant events, fade faster and that this differential fading is associated with happiness (Walker, Skowronski, & Thompson, 2003), that recalling positive autobiographical memories can repair an induced negative mood state (Joormann & Siemer, 2004), and that remembering positive events and forgetting nega-tive events is associated with increased well-being over the lifespan (Charles, Mather, & Carstensen, 2003). Studies investigating the use and effective-ness of mood-regulation strategies in depression suggest that in contrast to non-depressed persons, depressed individuals are unable to use positive autobiographical memories to regulate induced negative mood states (Joormann & Siemer, 2004; Joormann et al., 2007a). In two studies, we examined the formulation that dysphoria and rumination are critical factors in determining whether mood-congruent memory retrieval, as opposed to mood-repair processes, occurs (Joormann & Siemer, 2004). While non-dysphoric partici-pants’ mood ratings improved under distraction, as well as under mood-incongruent recall instruc-tions, dysphoric participants did not benefit from the recall of positive memories, while distraction seemed to alleviate their sad mood. In a recent study, we replicated these findings in a sample of currently depressed participants. Interestingly, pre-viously depressed participants exhibited similar difficulties in repairing their negative mood with positive memories (Joormann et al., 2007a). It is unclear at this point why mood-incongruent recall does not seem to work for depressed participants but it is possible that the recall of positive memories results in counterfactual thinking (e.g., a compar-ison of the current state with past good times) and rumination, which may induce negative affect. Future studies are needed to more closely look at the underlying mechanism of this effect. Overall,
JOORMANN AND D’AVANZATO
926 COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6)
the results are largely consistent with the literature on mood regulation (McFarland & Buehler, 1998; Rusting & DeHart, 2000) and support the notion that mood-incongruent recall is used as a mood-repair strategy in response to a negative mood induction. These results suggest that depression is associated with problems in employing an impor-tant emotion regulation strategy.
Individual differences in memory for emotional material may play an important role in explaining these difficulties. Memory biases such as increased accessibility of negative autobiographical material may lead to difficulties in accessing mood-incon-gruent material, which may interfere with the selection and use of effective emotion regulation strategies. Memory biases may also determine people’s perception of a specific situation, change their appraisals, and guide their attention towards specific aspects of that situation. Not surprisingly, preferential recall of negative compared to positive material is one of the most robust findings in the depression literature (Mathews & MacLeod, 2005; Matt, Vazquez, & Campbell, 1992). In a meta-analysis of studies assessing recall performance, Matt and colleagues found that people with major depression remember 10% more negative words than positive words. Non-depressed controls, in contrast, demonstrated a memory bias for positive information in 20 of 25 studies. It should be noted, however, that memory biases are found most consistently in free-recall tasks, and may also be restricted to explicit memory. Results using recog-nition or implicit memory measures have been much less conclusive (Watkins, 2002; see also Barry, Naus, & Lynn, 2004).
Depression is not only associated with en-hanced recall of negative events, but also with the recall of rather generic memories despite instruc-tions to recall specific events (i.e., overgeneral memory; see Williams et al., 2007, for a review). Furthermore, the extent to which an individual retrieves overgeneral memories predicted delayed recovery from affective disorders (e.g., Dalgleish, Spinks, Yiend, & Kuyken, 2001). Williams et al. (2007) proposed that individual differences in cognitive control and specifically in inhibitory dysfunction may underlie overgeneral recall in
depression, a proposition that we will examine more closely in the following paragraph. In addition, studies have shown rumination may maintain overgeneral memory in depressed pa-tients (Watkins & Teasdale, 2001, 2004). Under-standing overgeneral memory in the context of emotion regulation in depression may therefore be an important goal for future research. One particularly promising study found that training dysphoric individuals to be more concrete and less overgeneral in their thinking led to a significant reduction in depressive symptoms and rumination (Watkins, Baeyens, & Read, 2009).
In sum, memory biases are important to consider in depression. Depression is associated with increased accessibility of negative material and overgeneral memories, and depressed indivi-duals also exhibit difficulties in using an effective memory-based emotion regulation strategy, i.e., the recall of mood-incongruent material. In addition, mood-congruent recall and reduced accessibility of mood-incongruent material may contribute to difficulties using emotion regulation strategies such as reappraisal, but studies examin-ing this association are still needed.
COGNITIVE CONTROL AND INHIBITION
Reappraisal is an important emotion regulation strategy. We have already discussed different cognitive processes (attentional biases, memory biases) that may affect a person’s ability to use this strategy effectively. A critical cognitive process that affects individual differences in the ability to reappraise is cognitive control. Overriding pre-potent responses and inhibiting the processing of irrelevant material that captures attention are core abilities that allow us to respond flexibly and to adjust behaviour and emotional responses to changing situations. Cognitive control is related to the functioning of executive control processes such as inhibition in working memory (Hasher & Zacks, 1988; Hasher, Zacks, & May, 1999). Working memory is a limited-capacity system that provides temporary access to a select set of
EMOTION REGULATION IN DEPRESSION
COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6) 927
representations in the service of current cognitive processes (Cowan, 1999; Miyake & Shah, 1999). Thus, working memory reflects the focus of attention and the temporary activation of repre-sentations that are the contents of awareness. Given the capacity limitation of this system, it is important that the contents of working memory be updated efficiently, a task controlled by execu-tive processes (e.g., Friedman & Miyake, 2004; Hasher et al., 1999). Executive processes must selectively gate access to working memory, shield-ing it from intrusion from irrelevant material, as well as discard information that is no longer relevant. In this context, individual differences in the experience and resolution of interference are likely to affect cognitive and emotional function-ing. The occurrence of intrusive thoughts might be one consequence of poor interference resolu-tion. Several researchers have suggested that rumination and depression are associated with deficits in executive functioning (Hertel, 1997; Joormann, 2005; Linville, 1996).
Deficits in controlling the contents of working memory may affect emotion regulation because the experience of a mood state or an emotion is generally associated with the activation of mood-congruent representations in working memory (Isen, 1984; Siemer, 2005b). In addition, effective reappraisal may depend on a person’s ability to override (automatic) attention and interpretation biases that lead to unwanted appraisals of the emotion-eliciting cues. Replacing automatic ap-praisals with alternative evaluations of the situa-tion requires cognitive control. The ability to control the contents of working memory might therefore play an important role in emotion regulation. Thus, an inability to appropriately expel mood-congruent items from working mem-ory, as they become irrelevant, would lead to difficulties attending to and processing new information; and might also result in rumination and the use of other maladaptive emotion regula-tion strategies. Difficulties inhibiting salient but irrelevant thoughts and memories would also discourage the use of more effective emotion regulation strategies, such as reappraisal.
There is emerging evidence that depression is characterised by deficits in the inhibition of mood-congruent material. These deficits could result in prolonged processing of negative, goal-irrelevant aspects of presented information, thereby hinder-ing recovery from negative mood and leading to the sustained negative affect that characterises depressive episodes (Joormann, in press). The Negative Affective Priming task was designed to assess inhibition in the processing of emotional information (NAP; Joormann, 2004). This task assesses response times to positive and negative material that participants were instructed to ignore. Joormann (2004) found that dysphoric participants and participants with a history of depressive episodes exhibited reduced inhibition of negative material. Thus, these participants re-sponded faster when a negative target was pre-sented after a to-be-ignored negative distractor on the previous trial. As predicted, no group differ-ence was found for the positive adjectives. In a related study, participants who scored high on a self-report measure of rumination exhibited a reduced ability to inhibit the processing of emo-tional distractors, a finding that remained signifi-cant even after controlling for level of depressive symptoms (Joormann, 2006). Importantly, these findings were replicated using a negative priming task with emotional faces (Goeleven, DeRaedt, Baert, & Koster, 2006).
Negative priming tasks assess only one aspect of inhibition, that is the ability to control the access of relevant and irrelevant material to working mem-ory. In addition, there is an ongoing debate about the processes that underlie negative priming (e.g., Neill, Valdes, & Terry, 1995). Whereas these studies suggest that depression involves difficulties keeping irrelevant emotional information from entering working memory, depression may also be associated with difficulties removing previously relevant negative material from working memory. Difficulties inhibiting the processing of negative material that was, but is no longer, relevant might explain why people respond to negative mood states and negative life events with recurring, uncontrollable, and unintentional negative thoughts. To test this hypothesis, Joormann and
JOORMANN AND D’AVANZATO
928 COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6)
Gotlib (2008) used a modified Sternberg task that combines a short-term recognition task with instructions to ignore a previously memorised list of words to assess inhibition of irrelevant positive and negative stimuli. We found that participants diagnosed with major depression exhibited diffi-culties removing irrelevant negative material from working memory. Specifically, compared to never-depressed controls, depressed individuals exhibited longer decision latencies to an intrusion probe (i.e., a probe from the irrelevant list) than to a new probe (i.e., a completely new word), reflecting the strength of the residual activation of the contents of working memory that were declared to be no longer relevant. Importantly, this pattern was not found for positive material. Joormann and Gotlib also found that difficulty removing negative irrele-vant words from working memory was highly correlated with self-reported rumination, even after controlling for level of depressive symptoms. In sum, therefore, these findings indicate that depres-sion and rumination are associated with inhibitory impairments in the processing of emotional mate-rial specifically, with difficulties removing irrele-vant negative material from working memory. Finally, using a design in which participants are asked to resort material in working memory, Joormann, Levens, and Gotlib (2009) demon-strated that diagnosed depressed participants had difficulties manipulating negative material in working memory and that this deficit was asso-ciated with self-reported proneness to rumination.
Deficits in cognitive control may not only affect a person’s ability to discard irrelevant material from working memory, thereby increasing un-wanted thoughts, but these deficits may also make it difficult to intentionally forget unwanted mate-rial. The idea that depression is associated with these control deficits has been tested in directed forgetting tasks in which participants are in-structed to forget previously studied material at some point during the experiment. Later recall is tested, however, for material that was to be remembered and material that was to be forgotten (Bjork, 1972). Using positive and negative words, Power, Dalgleish, Claudio, Tata, and Kentish (2000) reported differential directed forgetting
effects for depressed and non-depressed partici-pants. Specifically, the depressed participants exhibited a facilitation effect for negative words after the ‘‘forget’’ instruction. It is important to note that the effect was only found when the adjectives were processed in a self-relevant manner. Hertel and Gerstle (2003) found that, compared with controls, dysphoric participants recalled more words they were supposed to forget, with a tendency towards increased recall of to-be-forgotten negative words. Moreover, the degree of forgetting was significantly correlated with self-report measures of rumination and unwanted thoughts. Finally, Joormann and Tran (2009) demonstrated that participants who scored high on a trait measure of rumination exhibited reduced forgetting of negative material in this task.
As outlined in the previous sections, deficits in inhibitory processes may play a central role in the occurrence of ruminative responses. Davis and Nolen-Hoeksema (2000) reported that ruminators made more errors on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) than did non-ruminators. Because the WCST measures executive control and cog-nitive flexibility, these results provide empirical support for the hypothesis that rumination is related to the executive control component of working memory. In addition, Joormann (2006) reported a correlation between rumination and deficits in cognitive inhibition as assessed by negative priming, and Joormann and Gotlib (2008) found a correlation between rumination and the ability to remove irrelevant negative material from working memory. Interestingly, studies that have manipulated rumination and have compared it to distraction have found that people who ruminated exhibited deficits in execu-tive control (Philippot & Brutoux, 2008; Watkins & Brown, 2002). These findings suggest that individual differences in executive control pro-cesses are closely associated with rumination. Deficits in executive control and inhibition are related to sustained processing of negative material and rumination, which in turn maintains the negative mood state and hinders recovery from negative affect. It is important to keep in mind, however, that the majority of studies investigating
EMOTION REGULATION IN DEPRESSION
COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6) 929
the relation between inhibition and rumination rely on correlational data, making it impossible to determine whether inhibition deficits are indeed causally linked to rumination. Further evidence for a close association between inhibition and rumina-tion comes from recent brain imaging studies. Investigators have found the combination of DLPFC hypoactivity and sustained amygdala activity to be related to self-reported rumination in a study that examined prolonged elaborative processing of emotional information in depression (Siegle, Steinhauer, Thase, Stenger, & Carter, 2002). In this study, while non-depressed indivi-duals exhibited amygdala responses to all stimuli that quickly decayed after offset, depressed in-dividuals were characterised by sustained amygdala responses to negative words. This sustained re-sponse lasted throughout the following non-emo-tional processing trials for depressed but not for control participants. Moreover, the difference in sustained amygdala activity to negative and posi-tive words was related to self-reported rumination.
Recently, studies have started to investigate the possibility of training cognitive control in depression and of examining the effects of this training on emotion regulation. Joormann, Hertel, Brozovich, and Gotlib (2005), for example, showed that depressed participants could be trained to forget negative material by practising active suppression and did particularly well when they were provided with a strategy of how to keep irrelevant material from entering working memory (i.e., by using thought substitutes; Joormann, Hertel, LeMoult, & Gotlib, 2009). Unfortunately, these authors did not investigate whether suppression training af-fected mood or emotional reactivity to a stressor. Siegle, Thompson, Carter, Steinhauer, and Thase (2007b), however, presented preliminary data demonstrating that a brief intervention targeted at increasing cognitive control in severely de-pressed out-patients led to significant decreases in both depressive symptoms and rumination. In-deed, recent work by this group suggests that training in attentional control may be an effective treatment component for depression (Siegle, Ghinassi, & Thase, 2007a). In this training, patients learn to selectively attend to certain
sounds while ignoring irrelevant sounds. After two weeks of this training, patients exhibited decreases in depressive symptoms compared to patients who received treatment as usual (Siegle et al., 2007a). Notably, the training consisted of short sessions (15 minutes) that used non-affective stimuli such as the sound of birds. This suggests that cognitive control can be improved with practice and further supports the hypothesis that individual differences in cognitive control may affect emotion regulation. In sum, these findings suggest that depression is asso-ciated with difficulties inhibiting negative irrele-vant material. As the central function of working memory, impaired inhibitory processes might have severe cognitive and emotional conse-quences, including rumination. Deficits in cogni-tive control may also make it difficult to employ attention flexibly, to override interpretive biases, and to use adaptive emotion regulation strategies such as reappraisal. Unfortunately, no studies to date have examined whether individual differ-ences in cognitive control affect people’s ability to use reappraisal. More research investigating the relation of cognitive control, executive functions, and inhibition on emotion regulation in depres-sion is clearly needed.
SUMMARY AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
Undoubtedly, depression is a heterogeneous dis-order that reflects a common endpoint for multiple pathways that lead to its development. It is highly unlikely, therefore, that a single causal pathway will explain a substantial amount of variability in this disorder. Still, difficulties in emotion regulation are an important characteristic of depressive disorders which may*in interaction with other factors* increase the risk for experiencing depressive epi-sodes. Underlying mechanisms of these difficulties need to be explored if we want to improve our understanding of this disorder as well as interven-tion and prevention efforts. In this article, we examined whether individual differences in cogni-tive processes have the potential to affect emotion
JOORMANN AND D’AVANZATO
930 COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6)
regulation and therefore play an important role in the onset and maintenance of depression. We have discussed numerous examples of how cognitive processes can hinder the selection and use of adaptive emotion regulation strategies such as attentional redirection, reappraisal, and mood-incongruent recall. We also provided some exam-ples of how these processes may be associated with the use of maladaptive regulation strategies such as rumination. Our review of the literature suggests that depression is characterised by difficulties disengaging from emotional material, by memory biases, and by deficits in cognitive control (see Figure 1). These biases may make it difficult for depressed people to use attentional deployment effectively, may reduce their ability to reappraise and may make it more likely that they ruminate when responding to negative affect. We also identified, however, that some strategies do not seem to work as well in people with depression. Depressed people, for example, cannot use mood-incongruent recall to repair their mood state, a strategy that works well in non-depressed partici-pants. So far, empirical studies addressing the effectiveness of various emotion regulation strate-gies in depression are largely missing.
Importantly, future research should directly investigate cognitive processes and emotional states in depression and should examine the causal impact of cognitive biases on difficulties in emotion regulation. Our brief review of the literature demonstrates that previous research has identified cognitive processes that characterise depression. As outlined previously, however, demonstrating that people diagnosed with depression differ from non-depressed controls in perception, attention, and memory is important but is not answering the question of whether biases affect the selection or effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies. Studies need to include measures of cognition, emotional responding, and emotion regulation within the same design and need to explore whether cognitive biases affect the use and effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies when confronted with emotion-eliciting situations. There are very few examples of studies that have begun to examine these processes. Studies on cognitive bias
modification, for example, demonstrate that changes in selective attention and automatic interpretation biases can affect people’s emotional responses when exposed to stressors. A minority of these studies, however, test the critical assumption that these changes in emotion responding are due to changes in the use of emotion regulation strategies when confronted with the stressor. This would require the examination of whether people in the training group do indeed differ from people in the control group in their use of emotion regulation strategies when encountering emotion-eliciting stimuli.
A particularly promising area of research that may help our understanding of underlying processes of emotion regulation in healthy and disordered people are neuroimaging studies (e.g., Beauregard, Levesque, & Bourgouin, 2001; Ochsner et al., 2002; see Ochsner & Gross, 2005, 2008, for reviews). These studies have shown, for example, that cognitive reappraisal inhibits activa-tion in subcortical regions that have been asso-ciated with emotion processing, including the amygdala and insula. Activation in these areas of the brain can be either up or down-regulated (i.e., increased or decreased) in accordance with the goal of reappraisal (Eippert et al., 2007; Goldin, McRae, Ramel, & Gross, 2008; Ochsner & Gross, 2005, 2008; Urry et al., 2006). For example, when reappraisal was used to decrease negative emo-tions, results indicated that the experience of negative emotion was reduced, and activity in the amygdala and insula was decreased (Goldin et al., 2008). Reappraisal is also associated with increases in activation in dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and prefrontal cortex, regions that are involved in working memory and long-term memory. During reappraisal, emotion-processing regions of the brain may become inversely coupled to the activa-tion of specific regions in the prefrontal cortex (Urry et al., 2006). These findings are consistent with the idea that reappraisal triggers top-down cognitive control of emotion-generating systems. Notably, reappraisal activates some of the same brain regions as tasks involving top-down atten-tion control (Ochsner et al., 2002), and the effects of reappraisal are partly explained by shifts in visual attention away from emotion-eliciting
EMOTION REGULATION IN DEPRESSION
COGNITION AND EMOTION, 2010, 24 (6) 931
stimuli (van Reekum et al., 2007). These findings support our proposition that reappraisal processes may be driven by attentional and cognitive control mechanisms. In addition, neuroimaging studies comparing distraction to reappraisal have found that these two strategies are supported by different areas of the brain, suggesting that people who claim to use reappraisal are not simply distracting themselves from negative stimuli (Kalisch et al., 2005; Kalisch, Wiech, Herrmann, & Dolan, 2006). These findings are exciting and represent first steps toward a more comprehensive model of how psychological and biological factors interact to facilitate or hinder emotion regulation, thereby affecting individuals’ vulnerability to experience depressive episodes.
Even though we tried to define and differ-entiate the main constructs that are the focus of our paper such as emotional reactivity, emotion regulation, and cognitive processes, there is nevertheless considerable overlap among defini-tions and much variability in how these con-structs are operationalised. Definitions of these constructs are often quite broad and over inclusive, which can lead to problems in assess-ment and in the consistency of theoretical models that propose relations among emotional reactivity, regulation, cognition, and psycho-pathology. More work is clearly needed to investigate the usefulness of the proposed defini-tions and to formulate cleaner, more specific, descriptions and operationalisations. Similar is-sues arise when trying to decide which processes to include under the label of ‘‘emotion regulation strategies’’. Rumination, for example, has been conceptualised as a cognitive process (Martin & Tesser, 1996) or as an acquired response style (Nolen-Hoeksema, 1991). Rumination in de-pression, however, is frequently initiated in response to negative affect in an attempt to cope with this affect and in an attempt to gain a deeper understanding of the situation that trig-gered the current mood state (Lyubomirsky & Nolen-Hoeksema, 1993). Along with other authors, we therefore think that it fits Gross’s definition of emotion regulation as strategies people use to attempt to influence how they
experience their emotions and can therefore be considered an emotion regulation strategy (Aldao, Nolen-Hoeksema, & Schweizer, 2010). Future research, however, is needed to further test this assumption.
At this point, a lot of questions remain unanswered. Why do people prefer certain emo-tion regulation strategies, and are people aware of this preference? Are certain strategies effective for some people but not others and, if so, why? Are individual differences in attention, interpretation, memory, and cognitive control indeed related to the selection and effectiveness of regulation strategies? How do people learn to use these strategies and how can we help them unlearn? Does modifying the types of strategies people use also in turn affect cognitive biases? Are the outlined associations among depression, cognitive processes, and emotion regulation specific to depressive disorders or a feature of psychopathol-ogy in general (Harvey, Watkins, Mansell, & Shafran, 2004)? These and other questions should be the main focus of future studies in this exciting area of research. Whereas current cognitive-behavioural treatments for depression have been shown to be the most effective treatments avail-able to address this debilitating disorder, there is still much room for improvement, specifically in reducing the risk of recurrent episodes and in reaching individuals who have not responded well to treatment. A deeper understanding of the ways that cognitive processes help and hinder emotion regulation may allow us to better address some of the difficulties depressed individuals encounter in developing new and more flexible ways of think-ing, a central goal of cognitive therapy. Under-standing the relation of cognitive processes and emotion regulation may also help us understand how we can get these new ways of thinking to ‘‘stick’’ to lead to permanent changes in emotional responding and to facilitate the use of these new skills in the face of stress.
